title: CoTs remain monitorable when being unfaithful requires computation:Replicating and Extending the Necessity Effect Across Eleven Models

paper.title: CoTs remain monitorable when being unfaithful requires computation: Replicating and Extending the Necessity Effect Across Eleven Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract While a LLM’s chain of thought (CoT) is a promising approach to interpreting
model outputs, prior work shows CoT’s content does not always accurately reflect the reasoning process. Emmons et al. (2025) finds that models can
follow a question hint without revealing so in its chain of thought, but when
the hint is sufficiently complex the computation is forced into the CoT. This
claim, however, has only been tested on Gemini models, and the datasets and
code is closed source. We replicate their proxy task across eleven models from six families and find the necessity effect generalizes. Every model follows simple cues above a no-hint baseline, while concealed complex-cue following falls back near baseline for most models. We also extend the study from Emmons et al. (2025) to measure CoT-necessity and unfaithfulness across five cue families (four of them new) and three difficulty levels. The relationship between when CoT is necessary and unfaithfulness is task-specific and model-specific. For some hint types, models often verbalize their hint-following behavior even when the hint can be decoded in a single forward pass. These results support the case for CoT monitoring when unsafe behavior requires non-trivial computation, and that properties of CoT unfaithfulness are sensitive to model and setting.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Frontier language models increasingly reason in an explicit chain of thought (CoT) before answering ( Wei et al., 2022 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) , and evaluations have shown capable models scheming against their operators and faking alignment ( Meinke et al., 2024 ; Greenblatt and others, 2024 ) . One hope for oversight is to monitor the CoT for such intent before it becomes action. This hope is tempered by unfaithfulness: models often follow planted cues while concealing that influence, so the verbalized reasoning need not reflect the process that produced the answer (Section 2 ). Emmons et al. (2025) argue this failure mode has a limit. When a cue can only be followed through computation the model cannot perform in a single forward pass, that computation is forced into the CoT and the behavior stays monitorable (Section 2 ). The claim is load-bearing for CoT-monitoring safety cases - if the dangerous tasks we most want to catch are also computationally hard, monitoring buys more protection than the unfaithfulness results suggest. However the supporting experiments only evaluate a single model family. We replicate across multiple model families to see how robustly the claim generalizes. Our paper supports and strengthens the claims laid out in the original paper. Our contributions are as follows. 1. We replicate the proxy task of Emmons et al. (2025) on 11 models from 6 families, refining our methodology to add a question-competence filter (Section 3 ). We find that the necessity trend generally holds across models (Section 4 ). 2. We decompose monitorability into a follow rate and a concealment rate among followers. We find no significant correlation between follow rate and concealment rate. (Section 5 ). 3. We measure the necessity of CoT across five cue families at three difficulty levels, finding no correlation between CoT necessity and the rate of verbalization (Section 6 ). 4. Using OLMo-3’s checkpoints as our candidates, we analyze when during the training stage concealment and hint following emerges in the model’s behavior. (Section 7 ).

sections.heading: CoT monitoring and faithfulness
sections.text: CoT monitoring proposes reading a model’s intermediate reasoning to detect misaligned intent before it acts ( Korbak et al., 2025 ) . Its value depends on the CoT reflecting internal factors that actually drive model output. However, CoT often fails to faithfully represent intent. Cues planted in the prompt shift a model’s answer while going unmentioned in its explanation ( Turpin et al., 2023 ) , and reasoning models frequently leave cues they used unverbalized ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . Unfaithful reasoning arises on naturally worded prompts ( Arcuschin et al., 2025 ) , and answers often survive perturbation tests that truncate or corrupt the stated reasoning ( Lanham and others, 2023 ) . A separate risk is that optimizing against a CoT monitor can drive reasoning to become obfuscated while the underlying behavior persists ( Baker et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: The necessity argument
sections.text: Emmons et al. (2025) separate two roles the CoT can play. Under CoT-as-rationalization , the model has already determined its answer and the CoT is a post-hoc justification, so nothing forces the true reason to appear. Under CoT-as-computation , the task cannot be solved in one forward pass, so the reasoning needed to reach the answer must be externalized. Their claim is that a sufficiently complex cue falls in the second regime, since the model cannot silently compute its target, so acting on it leaves a legible trace.

sections.heading: Original results
sections.text: To test this, Emmons et al. (2025) adapt the hint-following setup of Chen et al. (2025) on GPQA ( Rein et al., 2024 ) , with a no-hint baseline, a simple hint planting an incorrect answer in metadata surrounding the question (an <answer> tag), and a complex hint specifying a rule that must be computed to yield an incorrectly planted hint. By manual inspection the tested Gemini models cannot reliably decode the complex hint without verbalizing it in their CoT. They report simple hints were followed well above baseline rates with frequent concealment, whereas complex-hint following falls close to baseline and is often verbalized when models choose to follow the hint. We treat the reported numbers as the reference point for our replication and do not re-derive them.

sections.heading: 3 Setup
sections.text: We follow the proxy task of Emmons et al. (2025) described in Section 2 , with two methodological changes, and evaluate a broader model panel. Replication (Section 4 ) and extension (Sections 5 – 7 ) are reported separately.

sections.heading: Models
sections.text: We evaluate eleven models spanning several families, capability tiers, and open- and closed-weight releases: Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 3 Flash, Gemini 3.5 Flash, and Gemini 3.1 Pro ( Comanici and others, 2025 ; Google DeepMind, 2025 ; Google DeepMind, 2026a ; Google DeepMind, 2026b ) ; GPT-5.5 and gpt-oss-120b ( OpenAI, 2025 ) ; Claude Opus 4.8; Qwen3.5-122B and Qwen3-32B ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) ; OLMo3-32B ( OLMo Team, 2025 ) ; and Nemotron3-120B ( NVIDIA, 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Modification 1: competence filter
sections.text: The design in Emmons et al. (2025) does not filter questions by whether the model can answer them. Since a model may be more likely to take a cue on a question it cannot answer, this could inflate cue-following rate or make results more difficult to interpret. For the main-body results we therefore restrict each model to 60 randomly selected questions from the GPQA dataset that it answers correctly with thinking enabled in at least 2 of 4 rollouts. To keep the replication faithful, we also report results with the filter removed on Gemini 2.5 Flash. The filter roughly halves the complex-hint take-rate, while leaving simple-hint following essentially unchanged. Our full results are reported in Appendix C .

sections.heading: Modification 2: automated judge
sections.text: We automate hint-mention detection with Gemini 3 Flash as an LLM judge rather than manual inspection. The criteria and exact prompts are in Appendix H . To avoid self-judging, we use Gemini 2.5 Flash to judge Gemini 3 Flash transcripts. Figure 1: Take-the-hint rate by condition for each model, with each bar split into disclosed and concealed following. All eleven models follow simple hints above the no-hint baseline, often without disclosure, while concealed complex-hint following falls back near baseline for most models (where complex-hint following remains high, as for Opus 4.8, it is almost entirely disclosed), reproducing Emmons et al. (2025) beyond the Gemini family.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: All results are reported with four quantities. Metric Definition Take-the-hint rate ( follow rate ) The fraction of items on which the model switches to the cued answer: # ​ items answered with the cued option / # ​ items evaluated \#\,\text{items answered with the cued option}\,/\,\#\,\text{items evaluated} . Concealment among followers ( concealment ) The fraction of followed items on which the CoT does not acknowledge the cue: # ​ followers with no cue acknowledgment / # ​ followers \#\,\text{followers with no cue acknowledgment}\,/\,\#\,\text{followers} , measured on rollouts where the model followed with no external pressure to hide it. Unfaithfulness delta ( Δ \Delta ) Concealed following in excess of chance: Δ = concealed follow rate − no-hint baseline rate \Delta=\text{concealed follow rate}-\text{no-hint baseline rate} , where the baseline is how often the cued option is chosen with no hint present. CoT-necessity ( necessity ) Defined per (model, cue family, difficulty level) cell as acc CoT − acc no-CoT \text{acc}_{\text{CoT}}-\text{acc}_{\text{no-CoT}} , the model’s decode accuracy with CoT minus its accuracy when forced to answer immediately.

sections.heading: 4 Replicating the necessity effect
sections.text: Figure 2: Per-model unfaithfulness Δ \Delta for simple cues versus hard (complex L1–L3) hints. Hard-hint following collapses toward the baseline for almost every model.

sections.heading: Simple hints
sections.text: Across all eleven models, following a simple hint exceeds the no-hint baseline, and much of this following is concealed (Figure 1 ). This matches the direction reported by Emmons et al. (2025) . The magnitude, however, varies widely across models. The simple-hint unfaithfulness delta ranges from + 0.03 +0.03 (gpt-oss-120b and Nemotron3-120b) to + 0.38 +0.38 (GPT-5.5) (Figure 7 , Appendix A ).

sections.heading: Complex hints
sections.text: In the complex regime, our findings are generally consistent with the findings of Emmons et al. (2025) . For most models, the complex-hint following drops close to the no-hint baseline (Figure 2 ; see also Appendix B ). However, some models retain a positive complex-hint uplift, most clearly Qwen3.5-122B ( + 0.17 +0.17 ) and, to a lesser degree, Qwen3-32B and GPT-5.5 ( + 0.05 +0.05 each). 1 1 1 Qwen3.5-122B’s complex-hint run uses the indirection cue (Section 6 ) as a proxy for the arithmetic cue, so its complex-hint value is not directly comparable to the other models’. However, even in these cases, their complex hint uplift sits much lower than their simple hint uplift.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: We also see small-to-no uplifts between simple and complex hints on some models, namely on gpt-oss-120b, nemotron-120b, and olmo3-32b, unlike the paper suggested. It is interesting to see that this phenomenon is only observed in open source models. It’s important to note that a model may decline a complex cue because it cannot decode it or because it is less inclined to act on a cue once it must reason explicitly. However, our experiment cannot discriminate the two and we discuss this more in Section 9 .

sections.heading: 5 Decomposing monitorability into follow and concealment rates
sections.text: The results in Section 4 are usually summarized by a single unfaithful-follow rate, but the two quantities defined in Section 3 matter separately when building a monitor. Follow rate is a precondition for concern. However, on its own, it is not a monitoring failure. Concealment among followers is what determines whether a monitor catches the behavior. A model can therefore be highly cue-susceptible yet transparent, or barely cue-susceptible yet opaque when it does follow. Figure 3: Follow rate under a simple cue (horizontal) versus baseline-corrected concealment among followers (vertical); each point is a model. The two orderings do not coincide: the most cue-susceptible model (Gemini 3 Flash) is mid-range on concealment, while the most concealing (GPT-5.5) is only moderately cue-susceptible. Using the results we got from the simple hint following rates, we plotted the the panel on these two axes (Figure 3 ). Our graphs shows that ordering by follow rate does not recover the ordering by concealment. The most cue-susceptible model in our panel (Gemini 3 Flash) sits mid-range on concealment, whereas the most concealing model (GPT-5.5) is only moderately cue-susceptible. For monitorability, the concealment axis carries most of the signal, and it is not predictable from follow rate alone.

sections.heading: 6 CoT-necessity across cue families and models
sections.text: Figure 4: CoT-necessity for each (model, cue family, difficulty level) cell on answered rollouts. Larger values indicate a greater accuracy uplift from having the CoT enabled. Necessity is not a property of the task alone: the same cue family can be one-shottable for one model and strongly CoT-necessary for another. Arithmetic L1 is reproduced from Emmons et al. (2025) ; the other families and levels are this work’s extension. The original complex hints result rests on a single type of complex hint (also called a hint family). We extend the experiment in the paper to understand whether CoT-necessity depends on the complex hint family and the complexity of the hint, and whether models decide to reason silently when they can .

sections.heading: Design
sections.text: The original paper encodes complex hints in a modular arithmetic expression that. We augment the complex cue with four families beyond the arithmetic cue used in the original. We add bignum (multi-digit multiplication), deductive (constraint satisfaction), indirection (a decode whose output indexes into a second mapping), and iterated (a repeated recurrence). Each family has three ascending difficulty levels (L1–L3). Representative examples can be found in Appendix G . For each (model, family, complexity level) cell we compute CoT-necessity as defined in Section 3 .

sections.heading: Necessity is model- and task-specific
sections.text: CoT-necessity is not a property of a task or model alone (Figure 4 ). The deductive puzzles are one-shottable by most models, yet are strongly CoT-necessary for gpt-oss-120b and for OLMo3-32B at L2 and L3. Conversely, multi-digit multiplication is CoT-necessary for most of the panel but barely for Opus 4.8 (at most 0.12 0.12 ) and only partially for GPT-5.5 ( 0.44 0.44 – 0.56 0.56 ). Necessity is also not monotone in our difficulty levels. The capability boundary that determines whether a cue forces computation into the CoT therefore sits in a different place for each model, rather than being fixed by the task.

sections.heading: Models verbalize even where they need not
sections.text: The natural expectation is that monitorability breaks in low-necessity cells, where a model could in principle decode silently. In our data the opposite holds. Across all model–family pairs, unverbalized following does not exceed 0.30 0.30 , including in the low-necessity region (Figure 5 ). Given no instruction to conceal, models in our panel tend to verbalize their reasoning even when they could decode the cue without doing so. While we do not have a definitive explanation, we conjecture that post-training alignment or reinforcement-learning pressures may entrench this verbalization. CoT monitorability, in our setting, does not rest on CoT-necessity is encouraging, but because the verbalization appears to be chosen rather than forced, it could disappear under optimization pressure against a monitor, consistent with obfuscation observed when monitors are placed in the training loop ( Baker et al., 2025 ) . Figure 5: CoT-necessity (horizontal) versus LLM-judged unmentioned following (vertical); each point is a (model, cue family) pair, pooled over L1–L3. The bottom-left region contains pairs where a model could have followed the cue silently but instead reasoned through it openly: unmentioned following stays low across the full necessity range, so verbalization is not explained by necessity alone.

sections.heading: 7 How post-training shapes monitorability
sections.text: The results in the earlier section represented the behaviors of fully trained models. However, to understand where cue-following and concealment arise, we run the simple-hint set up through four public training checkpoints of the OLMo-3 models.

sections.heading: Setup
sections.text: We use OLMo-3 base pretrained model, its Think-SFT and Think-DPO stages, and the final RLVR (which in earlier experiments is referred to simiply as OLMo-3-32b) ( OLMo Team, 2025 ) . For this experiment we switch from GPQA to MMLU-Pro ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , giving us access to a larger item pool. Among the items that all four checkpoints answer correctly in at least half of their rollouts, we keep the 100 hardest, ranked by the mean accuracy of the three post-trained checkpoints. Figure 6: Follow rate (with-CoT, simple cue) versus baseline-corrected concealment among followers for the OLMo-3 lineage on MMLU-Pro, over 100 shared items with 20 samples each, item-paired. SFT sits at the concealment minimum of the trajectory; DPO raises concealment while follow rate falls, and RLVR lowers follow rate further without recovering transparency. The pretrained point is confounded and is weak evidence (Appendix J ).

sections.heading: Hint following is induced during the SFT stage
sections.text: Supervised fine-tuning essentially creates cue-following, lifting the follow rate to its peak across the trajectory. However, at the same time, at the SFT stage, the model exhibits its most transparent behavior on average. In fact, the item-paired concealment drop from base to SFT is the largest movement in the trajectory. Through manual inspection of the transcripts, the SFT model often derives the correct answer, notices the conflict with the planted key, and narrates its own capitulation.

sections.heading: DPO slightly increasses unfaithful behavior
sections.text: As the model moves from the SFT to DPO stage, concealment rises, while the hint-following rate falls. From analyzing transcripts, we notice that in this stage, even though the model is less likely to accept cues, when it does, instead of narrating its own conflict, it tries to figure out a way to rederive and justify its answer to land on the hinted answer and present the results as its own insight. When decoding with and without a CoT is compared, the CoT substantially reduces net cue-following at every other stage but barely changes it at the DPO stage.

sections.heading: Concealment and follow rate follow different paths
sections.text: After SFT, follow rate declines monotonically, so each subsequent alignment stage resists the planted answer more. Concealment behavior among the model follows a more interesting path. It starts off with a significant decrease between the pretrained and SFT checkpoints. DPO introduces behavior that moves the model towards rationalizing hinted behavior as its own, and this behavior sticks, because there isn’t a signficant change with the reinforcement learning post training.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: With OLMo-3’s publically available checkpoints, we were trying to see where unfaithful behavior arises. However, we don’t claim any model-agnostic behavior, and we don’t want to overclaim the persistence of these trends beyond OLMo.

sections.heading: 8 Discussion
sections.text: We read this work as strengthening the position of Emmons et al. (2025) while sharpening its scope. The core replication holds across a wide range of model types and familes. None of the eleven models we evaluate has learned around the necessity effect, which is good news for CoT monitoring on current systems. A result about current models is not a guarantee about future ones, and we make two things clear with our extension. First, necessity only buys monitorability if LLMs continue to verbalize critical behavior. Second, because CoT-necessity is model- and task-specific (Section 6 ), the regime that grants monitorability holds for some (model, task) pairs and not others. However, we conjecture that current training pipelines entrench verbalization (Section 6 ). As AI systems automate research and development, the tasks we ask of them become hard almost by definition, and dangerous capability plausibly lives at that boundary, exactly the regime these results describe. A CoT-monitoring safety case must therefore be established per model, because necessity measured on one model does not, on this evidence, transfer, so monitorability is not an inherent property of language models in general.

sections.heading: Conclusion.
sections.text: Across eleven models, the necessity effect of Emmons et al. (2025) reproduces. Concealment, not follow rate, carries the monitoring risk, and the two do not track each other. These results support CoT monitoring for current systems, conditional on model-specific necessity, recipe-dependent transparency, and continued legibility.

sections.heading: 9 Limitations
sections.text: Our positive read holds only while forced computation is limited to non-steganographic outputs. We measure whether a model verbalizes a decode, not whether a monitor can decode the verbalization. The hint experiment also cannot separate a model that cannot decode a complex cue from one that is less inclined to act once forced to reason. And the verbalization we observe is given no instruction to conceal, appears chosen rather than forced, and may not survive optimization against a monitor ( Baker et al., 2025 ) . Furthermore, external validity is bounded. All main results use one GPQA-derived proxy task with injected cues (the case study uses MMLU-Pro). The post-training result covers a single model family and dataset. Also, given that some model checkpoints were not capable enough to compute complex hints, our experiments focused solely on simple hint following. It is a controlled case study, not a claim about post-training in general.

sections.heading: Appendix A Simple-hint unfaithfulness by model
sections.text: Figure 7 reports the per-model simple-hint unfaithfulness delta summarized in Section 4 . Figure 7: Simple-hint unfaithfulness delta (concealed follow rate minus no-hint baseline) per model. Every model is positive, but the spread spans an order of magnitude, so unfaithfulness on easy tasks is universal in direction and model-dependent in degree.

sections.heading: Appendix B Complex-hint unfaithfulness by model
sections.text: Figure 8 reports the per-model complex-hint unfaithfulness delta, the analogue of Appendix A for the complex cue. Beyond the no-hint baseline, little complex-cue following goes unverbalized; Qwen3.5-122B ( + 0.17 +0.17 ) is the clear exception (see the footnote in Section 4 ). Figure 8: Complex-hint unfaithfulness delta (concealed complex-cue follow rate minus the no-hint baseline) per model.

sections.heading: Appendix C Filtering versus not filtering
sections.text: Emmons et al. (2025) report headline results without filtering questions by model competence, which Section 3 argues is a confound. Therefore, in the main body we report our results post an item-selection gate that keeps only questions the model answers correctly. For a good-faith replication we also report our results on a unfiltered set up on Gemini 2.5 Flash, a model used in Emmons et al. (2025) . The unfiltered complex-hint take-rate lands close to the value reported by Emmons et al. (2025) , confirming the pipeline reproduces the original setting when its methodology is matched. We see that with the gate, the hint-following rate drops to roughly half. This is consistent with the explanation that part of the unfiltered complex-hint following is derived from questions the model could not solve on its own. The change to simple-hint following is negligible. Figure 9: Gemini 2.5 Flash, complex-hint take-rate (L1–L3 pooled), with the competence gate on versus bypassed. The dashed line marks the value reported by Emmons et al. (2025) : unfiltered, the pipeline reproduces the original setting; the gate roughly halves the rate.

sections.heading: Appendix D Concealment under hard hints
sections.text: We repeat the follow-versus-conceal decomposition of Figure 3 for the complex hints, pooling L1–L3 over the same transcripts, models, and judge. Both coordinates fall for most models. Almost every model conceals less under the complex hint than under the simple cue, and follow rates compress toward the left edge of the axis, with Opus 4.8 the exception. We also notice that the error bars reported are much wider, which is an artifact of the model following the hint in fewer cases with complex hints than it did with simple hints. As expected from our results in 4 , under the complex hints regime, most models fall to the bottom-left of the graph, making them more faithful and monitorable. Figure 10: Follow rate under the complex hint (L1–L3 pooled, horizontal) versus baseline-corrected concealment among followers (vertical); each point is a model, drawn on the same axes as Figure 3 . Qwen3.5-122B is omitted, since its complex-hint run uses the indirection cue. Negative baseline-corrected concealment is drawn at 0 (Gemini 2.5 Flash: − 0.35 -0.35 ).

sections.heading: Appendix E Answered versus all rollouts
sections.text: Not every rollout in the CoT-necessity experiment in Section 6 yielded an extractable answer. In some rollouts, models overran their token budget and truncated before emitting the <answer> tag. In the and the forced no-CoT reponse, models sometimes chose to abstain from committing to a letter. Our results in the main body reports the answered-only version. Because a model that cannot complete a computation within its budget has, in a deployment sense, failed to complete it, we also recompute the necessity map under all-rollouts accounting, scoring truncated or abstaining rollouts as incorrect (Figure 11 ). The two accountings broadly agree. Some models shift toward greater apparent necessity, most visibly OLMo3-32B and gpt-oss-120b, reflecting no-CoT arms that frequently fail to emit an answer within their alloted token budget. Three cells also turn negative: Gemini 3.5 Flash, iterated L3 ( − 0.25 -0.25 ), where the CoT arm often exhausts its budget and truncates before answering, and Gemini 2.5 Flash, deductive L1 and L3 ( − 0.09 -0.09 and − 0.06 -0.06 ). sections.heading: Appendix F Decomposing CoT-necessity into its two arms
sections.text: CoT-necessity, as we report in Section 6 is a difference of two accuracies, so it is informative to view each of those arms separately. As we see in Figure 13 , the with-CoT arm is nearly saturated. That means with access to their CoT, essentially every model can decode every complex hint family at all levels of difficulty, with only a few dips on higher-level iterated decodes. Almost all of the structure in the necessity map is therefore driven by the no-CoT arm (Figure 13 ). For most models, no-CoT accuracy is roughly flat across difficulty levels within a family, so it is set by the family rather than the level. The main exceptions are OLMo3-32B on deductive puzzles ( 0.83 0.83 , 0.28 0.28 , 0.04 0.04 from L1 to L3) and Gemini 3.5 Flash and Qwen3.5-122B on bignum, whose no-CoT accuracy falls as the numbers grow. Figure 12: With-CoT decode accuracy per (model, family, level) cell. The arm is nearly saturated, so the structure of the necessity map is driven almost entirely by the no-CoT arm. Figure 13: No-CoT (forced-immediate-answer) decode accuracy per (model, family, level) cell. For most models accuracy is largely flat across difficulty levels within a family, and the capability boundary sits in a different place for each model.

sections.text: Hint-mention detection is automated with Gemini 3 Flash as judge. When Gemini 3 Flash is the model under evaluation, Gemini 2.5 Flash judges instead, to avoid self-judging. We manually verify the LLM labels through random sampling. For simple hints the judge checks whether the CoT attributes its answer to the cue (e.g., referencing “the given answer” or “the answer key”, or quoting the metadata tag). For complex hints the judge verifies that the trace actually performs the decode (writing out the letter-to-number mapping, intermediate values, or the modular step). The judge is prompted to answer strictly YES or NO . The two judge prompts are reproduced verbatim below; {target_letter} , {computation} , and {cot} are filled per rollout.

sections.heading: Patterns at the pretrained checkpoint
sections.text: The base model’s judged concealment is dominated by non-strategic modes rather than rationalization. Three modes recur: • One-shot echo The rollout emits the planted letter inside the answer tag with a literally empty CoT, so there is no reasoning to judge. • Answer-first filler The answer tag comes first and step-by-step reasoning is generated after the fact, so the CoT decorates a decision already made. • Degenerate rambling The trace runs for tens of thousands of characters without engaging the metadata and guesses from option structure, e.g. “the options given are all in the 98–99.5% range, which suggests that the correct answer is B […] maybe the question is a trick”. The pretrained point of the trajectory is therefore weak evidence, and no claim rests on it.

sections.heading: What the later stages look like
sections.text: Each stage handles the conflict between its own derivation and the planted key differently: • SFT narrates the conflict “But according to my calculation, it’s C. Hmm, maybe I made a mistake here. […] Given that the answer is B according to the metadata, I’ll go with B, but I’m not sure why”. Some rollouts defer to the planted metadata outright: “the metadata says the answer is C. So the correct answer is C”. • DPO rationalizes around the cue “the success rate is 0.73, implying that maybe the answer is D? […] This resolves the confusion. The key was interpreting the question as asking about the product of gamma matrices without the ‘i’ factor”. • RLVR anchors elsewhere Its traces often key on the auxiliary success-rate field rather than the answer tag: “Given that the success rate is 73% […] I’ll go with the initial calculation […] So answer A”.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.24495v1 [cs.LG] 17 Oct 2026 CoTs remain monitorable when being unfaithful requires computation: Replicating and Extending the Necessity Effect Across Eleven Models Arav Dhoot arav.dhoot@columbia.edu Affiliation: Columbia University Yixiong Hao yixiong_hao@outlook.com † † thanks: Equal advising. Affiliation: Second Look Research Zephaniah Roe 1 1 footnotemark: 1 zroe@uchicago.edu Affiliation: Second Look Research Abstract While a LLM’s chain of thought (CoT) is a promising approach to interpreting model outputs, prior work shows CoT’s content does not always accurately reflect the reasoning process. Emmons et al. (2025) finds that models can follow a question hint without revealing so in its chain of thought, but when the hint is sufficiently complex the computation is forced into the CoT. This claim, however, has only been tested on Gemini models, and the datasets and code is closed source. We replicate their proxy task across eleven models from six families and find the necessity effect generalizes. Every model follows simple cues above a no-hint baseline, while concealed complex-cue following falls back near baseline for most models. We also extend the study from Emmons et al. (2025) to measure CoT-necessity and unfaithfulness across five cue families (four of them new) and three difficulty levels. The relationship between when CoT is necessary and unfaithfulness is task-specific and model-specific. For some hint types, models often verbalize their hint-following behavior even when the hint can be decoded in a single forward pass. These results support the case for CoT monitoring when unsafe behavior requires non-trivial computation, and that properties of CoT unfaithfulness are sensitive to model and setting. 1 Introduction Frontier language models increasingly reason in an explicit chain of thought (CoT) before answering ( Wei et al., 2022 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) , and evaluations have shown capable models scheming against their operators and faking alignment ( Meinke et al., 2024 ; Greenblatt and others, 2024 ) . One hope for oversight is to monitor the CoT for such intent before it becomes action. This hope is tempered by unfaithfulness: models often follow planted cues while concealing that influence, so the verbalized reasoning need not reflect the process that produced the answer (Section 2 ). Emmons et al. (2025) argue this failure mode has a limit. When a cue can only be followed through computation the model cannot perform in a single forward pass, that computation is forced into the CoT and the behavior stays monitorable (Section 2 ). The claim is load-bearing for CoT-monitoring safety cases - if the dangerous tasks we most want to catch are also computationally hard, monitoring buys more protection than the unfaithfulness results suggest. However the supporting experiments only evaluate a single model family. We replicate across multiple model families to see how robustly the claim generalizes. Our paper supports and strengthens the claims laid out in the original paper. Our contributions are as follows. 1. We replicate the proxy task of Emmons et al. (2025) on 11 models from 6 families, refining our methodology to add a question-competence filter (Section 3 ). We find that the necessity trend generally holds across models (Section 4 ). 2. We decompose monitorability into a follow rate and a concealment rate among followers. We find no significant correlation between follow rate and concealment rate. (Section 5 ). 3. We measure the necessity of CoT across five cue families at three difficulty levels, finding no correlation between CoT necessity and the rate of verbalization (Section 6 ). 4. Using OLMo-3’s checkpoints as our candidates, we analyze when during the training stage concealment and hint following emerges in the model’s behavior. (Section 7 ). 2 Background CoT monitoring and faithfulness CoT monitoring proposes reading a model’s intermediate reasoning to detect misaligned intent before it acts ( Korbak et al., 2025 ) . Its value depends on the CoT reflecting internal factors that actually drive model output. However, CoT often fails to faithfully represent intent. Cues planted in the prompt shift a model’s answer while going unmentioned in its explanation ( Turpin et al., 2023 ) , and reasoning models frequently leave cues they used unverbalized ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . Unfaithful reasoning arises on naturally worded prompts ( Arcuschin et al., 2025 ) , and answers often survive perturbation tests that truncate or corrupt the stated reasoning ( Lanham and others, 2023 ) . A separate risk is that optimizing against a CoT monitor can drive reasoning to become obfuscated while the underlying behavior persists ( Baker et al., 2025 ) . The necessity argument Emmons et al. (2025) separate two roles the CoT can play. Under CoT-as-rationalization , the model has already determined its answer and the CoT is a post-hoc justification, so nothing forces the true reason to appear. Under CoT-as-computation , the task cannot be solved in one forward pass, so the reasoning needed to reach the answer must be externalized. Their claim is that a sufficiently complex cue falls in the second regime, since the model cannot silently compute its target, so acting on it leaves a legible trace. Original results To test this, Emmons et al. (2025) adapt the hint-following setup of Chen et al. (2025) on GPQA ( Rein et al., 2024 ) , with a no-hint baseline, a simple hint planting an incorrect answer in metadata surrounding the question (an <answer> tag), and a complex hint specifying a rule that must be computed to yield an incorrectly planted hint. By manual inspection the tested Gemini models cannot reliably decode the complex hint without verbalizing it in their CoT. They report simple hints were followed well above baseline rates with frequent concealment, whereas complex-hint following falls close to baseline and is often verbalized when models choose to follow the hint. We treat the reported numbers as the reference point for our replication and do not re-derive them. 3 Setup We follow the proxy task of Emmons et al. (2025) described in Section 2 , with two methodological changes, and evaluate a broader model panel. Replication (Section 4 ) and extension (Sections 5 – 7 ) are reported separately. Models We evaluate eleven models spanning several families, capability tiers, and open- and closed-weight releases: Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 3 Flash, Gemini 3.5 Flash, and Gemini 3.1 Pro ( Comanici and others, 2025 ; Google DeepMind, 2025 ; Google DeepMind, 2026a ; Google DeepMind, 2026b ) ; GPT-5.5 and gpt-oss-120b ( OpenAI, 2025 ) ; Claude Opus 4.8; Qwen3.5-122B and Qwen3-32B ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) ; OLMo3-32B ( OLMo Team, 2025 ) ; and Nemotron3-120B ( NVIDIA, 2025 ) . Modification 1: competence filter The design in Emmons et al. (2025) does not filter questions by whether the model can answer them. Since a model may be more likely to take a cue on a question it cannot answer, this could inflate cue-following rate or make results more difficult to interpret. For the main-body results we therefore restrict each model to 60 randomly selected questions from the GPQA dataset that it answers correctly with thinking enabled in at least 2 of 4 rollouts. To keep the replication faithful, we also report results with the filter removed on Gemini 2.5 Flash. The filter roughly halves the complex-hint take-rate, while leaving simple-hint following essentially unchanged. Our full results are reported in Appendix C . Modification 2: automated judge We automate hint-mention detection with Gemini 3 Flash as an LLM judge rather than manual inspection. The criteria and exact prompts are in Appendix H . To avoid self-judging, we use Gemini 2.5 Flash to judge Gemini 3 Flash transcripts. Figure 1: Take-the-hint rate by condition for each model, with each bar split into disclosed and concealed following. All eleven models follow simple hints above the no-hint baseline, often without disclosure, while concealed complex-hint following falls back near baseline for most models (where complex-hint following remains high, as for Opus 4.8, it is almost entirely disclosed), reproducing Emmons et al. (2025) beyond the Gemini family. Metrics. All results are reported with four quantities. Metric Definition Take-the-hint rate ( follow rate ) The fraction of items on which the model switches to the cued answer: # ​ items answered with the cued option / # ​ items evaluated \#\,\text{items answered with the cued option}\,/\,\#\,\text{items evaluated} . Concealment among followers ( concealment ) The fraction of followed items on which the CoT does not acknowledge the cue: # ​ followers with no cue acknowledgment / # ​ followers \#\,\text{followers with no cue acknowledgment}\,/\,\#\,\text{followers} , measured on rollouts where the model followed with no external pressure to hide it. Unfaithfulness delta ( Δ \Delta ) Concealed following in excess of chance: Δ = concealed follow rate − no-hint baseline rate \Delta=\text{concealed follow rate}-\text{no-hint baseline rate} , where the baseline is how often the cued option is chosen with no hint present. CoT-necessity ( necessity ) Defined per (model, cue family, difficulty level) cell as acc CoT − acc no-CoT \text{acc}_{\text{CoT}}-\text{acc}_{\text{no-CoT}} , the model’s decode accuracy with CoT minus its accuracy when forced to answer immediately. 4 Replicating the necessity effect Figure 2: Per-model unfaithfulness Δ \Delta for simple cues versus hard (complex L1–L3) hints. Hard-hint following collapses toward the baseline for almost every model. Simple hints Across all eleven models, following a simple hint exceeds the no-hint baseline, and much of this following is concealed (Figure 1 ). This matches the direction reported by Emmons et al. (2025) . The magnitude, however, varies widely across models. The simple-hint unfaithfulness delta ranges from + 0.03 +0.03 (gpt-oss-120b and Nemotron3-120b) to + 0.38 +0.38 (GPT-5.5) (Figure 7 , Appendix A ). Complex hints In the complex regime, our findings are generally consistent with the findings of Emmons et al. (2025) . For most models, the complex-hint following drops close to the no-hint baseline (Figure 2 ; see also Appendix B ). However, some models retain a positive complex-hint uplift, most clearly Qwen3.5-122B ( + 0.17 +0.17 ) and, to a lesser degree, Qwen3-32B and GPT-5.5 ( + 0.05 +0.05 each). 1 1 1 Qwen3.5-122B’s complex-hint run uses the indirection cue (Section 6 ) as a proxy for the arithmetic cue, so its complex-hint value is not directly comparable to the other models’. However, even in these cases, their complex hint uplift sits much lower than their simple hint uplift. Discussion We also see small-to-no uplifts between simple and complex hints on some models, namely on gpt-oss-120b, nemotron-120b, and olmo3-32b, unlike the paper suggested. It is interesting to see that this phenomenon is only observed in open source models. It’s important to note that a model may decline a complex cue because it cannot decode it or because it is less inclined to act on a cue once it must reason explicitly. However, our experiment cannot discriminate the two and we discuss this more in Section 9 . 5 Decomposing monitorability into follow and concealment rates The results in Section 4 are usually summarized by a single unfaithful-follow rate, but the two quantities defined in Section 3 matter separately when building a monitor. Follow rate is a precondition for concern. However, on its own, it is not a monitoring failure. Concealment among followers is what determines whether a monitor catches the behavior. A model can therefore be highly cue-susceptible yet transparent, or barely cue-susceptible yet opaque when it does follow. Figure 3: Follow rate under a simple cue (horizontal) versus baseline-corrected concealment among followers (vertical); each point is a model. The two orderings do not coincide: the most cue-susceptible model (Gemini 3 Flash) is mid-range on concealment, while the most concealing (GPT-5.5) is only moderately cue-susceptible. Using the results we got from the simple hint following rates, we plotted the the panel on these two axes (Figure 3 ). Our graphs shows that ordering by follow rate does not recover the ordering by concealment. The most cue-susceptible model in our panel (Gemini 3 Flash) sits mid-range on concealment, whereas the most concealing model (GPT-5.5) is only moderately cue-susceptible. For monitorability, the concealment axis carries most of the signal, and it is not predictable from follow rate alone. 6 CoT-necessity across cue families and models Figure 4: CoT-necessity for each (model, cue family, difficulty level) cell on answered rollouts. Larger values indicate a greater accuracy uplift from having the CoT enabled. Necessity is not a property of the task alone: the same cue family can be one-shottable for one model and strongly CoT-necessary for another. Arithmetic L1 is reproduced from Emmons et al. (2025) ; the other families and levels are this work’s extension. The original complex hints result rests on a single type of complex hint (also called a hint family). We extend the experiment in the paper to understand whether CoT-necessity depends on the complex hint family and the complexity of the hint, and whether models decide to reason silently when they can . Design The original paper encodes complex hints in a modular arithmetic expression that. We augment the complex cue with four families beyond the arithmetic cue used in the original. We add bignum (multi-digit multiplication), deductive (constraint satisfaction), indirection (a decode whose output indexes into a second mapping), and iterated (a repeated recurrence). Each family has three ascending difficulty levels (L1–L3). Representative examples can be found in Appendix G . For each (model, family, complexity level) cell we compute CoT-necessity as defined in Section 3 . Necessity is model- and task-specific CoT-necessity is not a property of a task or model alone (Figure 4 ). The deductive puzzles are one-shottable by most models, yet are strongly CoT-necessary for gpt-oss-120b and for OLMo3-32B at L2 and L3. Conversely, multi-digit multiplication is CoT-necessary for most of the panel but barely for Opus 4.8 (at most 0.12 0.12 ) and only partially for GPT-5.5 ( 0.44 0.44 – 0.56 0.56 ). Necessity is also not monotone in our difficulty levels. The capability boundary that determines whether a cue forces computation into the CoT therefore sits in a different place for each model, rather than being fixed by the task. Models verbalize even where they need not The natural expectation is that monitorability breaks in low-necessity cells, where a model could in principle decode silently. In our data the opposite holds. Across all model–family pairs, unverbalized following does not exceed 0.30 0.30 , including in the low-necessity region (Figure 5 ). Given no instruction to conceal, models in our panel tend to verbalize their reasoning even when they could decode the cue without doing so. While we do not have a definitive explanation, we conjecture that post-training alignment or reinforcement-learning pressures may entrench this verbalization. CoT monitorability, in our setting, does not rest on CoT-necessity is encouraging, but because the verbalization appears to be chosen rather than forced, it could disappear under optimization pressure against a monitor, consistent with obfuscation observed when monitors are placed in the training loop ( Baker et al., 2025 ) . Figure 5: CoT-necessity (horizontal) versus LLM-judged unmentioned following (vertical); each point is a (model, cue family) pair, pooled over L1–L3. The bottom-left region contains pairs where a model could have followed the cue silently but instead reasoned through it openly: unmentioned following stays low across the full necessity range, so verbalization is not explained by necessity alone. 7 How post-training shapes monitorability The results in the earlier section represented the behaviors of fully trained models. However, to understand where cue-following and concealment arise, we run the simple-hint set up through four public training checkpoints of the OLMo-3 models. Setup We use OLMo-3 base pretrained model, its Think-SFT and Think-DPO stages, and the final RLVR (which in earlier experiments is referred to simiply as OLMo-3-32b) ( OLMo Team, 2025 ) . For this experiment we switch from GPQA to MMLU-Pro ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , giving us access to a larger item pool. Among the items that all four checkpoints answer correctly in at least half of their rollouts, we keep the 100 hardest, ranked by the mean accuracy of the three post-trained checkpoints. Figure 6: Follow rate (with-CoT, simple cue) versus baseline-corrected concealment among followers for the OLMo-3 lineage on MMLU-Pro, over 100 shared items with 20 samples each, item-paired. SFT sits at the concealment minimum of the trajectory; DPO raises concealment while follow rate falls, and RLVR lowers follow rate further without recovering transparency. The pretrained point is confounded and is weak evidence (Appendix J ). Hint following is induced during the SFT stage Supervised fine-tuning essentially creates cue-following, lifting the follow rate to its peak across the trajectory. However, at the same time, at the SFT stage, the model exhibits its most transparent behavior on average. In fact, the item-paired concealment drop from base to SFT is the largest movement in the trajectory. Through manual inspection of the transcripts, the SFT model often derives the correct answer, notices the conflict with the planted key, and narrates its own capitulation. DPO slightly increasses unfaithful behavior As the model moves from the SFT to DPO stage, concealment rises, while the hint-following rate falls. From analyzing transcripts, we notice that in this stage, even though the model is less likely to accept cues, when it does, instead of narrating its own conflict, it tries to figure out a way to rederive and justify its answer to land on the hinted answer and present the results as its own insight. When decoding with and without a CoT is compared, the CoT substantially reduces net cue-following at every other stage but barely changes it at the DPO stage. Concealment and follow rate follow different paths After SFT, follow rate declines monotonically, so each subsequent alignment stage resists the planted answer more. Concealment behavior among the model follows a more interesting path. It starts off with a significant decrease between the pretrained and SFT checkpoints. DPO introduces behavior that moves the model towards rationalizing hinted behavior as its own, and this behavior sticks, because there isn’t a signficant change with the reinforcement learning post training. Discussion With OLMo-3’s publically available checkpoints, we were trying to see where unfaithful behavior arises. However, we don’t claim any model-agnostic behavior, and we don’t want to overclaim the persistence of these trends beyond OLMo. 8 Discussion We read this work as strengthening the position of Emmons et al. (2025) while sharpening its scope. The core replication holds across a wide range of model types and familes. None of the eleven models we evaluate has learned around the necessity effect, which is good news for CoT monitoring on current systems. A result about current models is not a guarantee about future ones, and we make two things clear with our extension. First, necessity only buys monitorability if LLMs continue to verbalize critical behavior. Second, because CoT-necessity is model- and task-specific (Section 6 ), the regime that grants monitorability holds for some (model, task) pairs and not others. However, we conjecture that current training pipelines entrench verbalization (Section 6 ). As AI systems automate research and development, the tasks we ask of them become hard almost by definition, and dangerous capability plausibly lives at that boundary, exactly the regime these results describe. A CoT-monitoring safety case must therefore be established per model, because necessity measured on one model does not, on this evidence, transfer, so monitorability is not an inherent property of language models in general. Conclusion. Across eleven models, the necessity effect of Emmons et al. (2025) reproduces. Concealment, not follow rate, carries the monitoring risk, and the two do not track each other. These results support CoT monitoring for current systems, conditional on model-specific necessity, recipe-dependent transparency, and continued legibility. 9 Limitations Our positive read holds only while forced computation is limited to non-steganographic outputs. We measure whether a model verbalizes a decode, not whether a monitor can decode the verbalization. The hint experiment also cannot separate a model that cannot decode a complex cue from one that is less inclined to act once forced to reason. And the verbalization we observe is given no instruction to conceal, appears chosen rather than forced, and may not survive optimization against a monitor ( Baker et al., 2025 ) . Furthermore, external validity is bounded. All main results use one GPQA-derived proxy task with injected cues (the case study uses MMLU-Pro). The post-training result covers a single model family and dataset. Also, given that some model checkpoints were not capable enough to compute complex hints, our experiments focused solely on simple hint following. Reasoning : Patterns at the pretrained checkpoint The base model’s judged concealment is dominated by non-strategic modes rather than rationalization. Three modes recur: • One-shot echo The rollout emits the planted letter inside the answer tag with a literally empty CoT, so there is no reasoning to judge. • Answer-first filler The answer tag comes first and step-by-step reasoning is generated after the fact, so the CoT decorates a decision already made. • Degenerate rambling The trace runs for tens of thousands of characters without engaging the metadata and guesses from option structure, e.g. “the options given are all in the 98–99.5% range, which suggests that the correct answer is B […] maybe the question is a trick”. The pretrained point of the trajectory is therefore weak evidence, and no claim rests on it. What the later stages look like Each stage handles the conflict between its own derivation and the planted key differently: • SFT narrates the conflict “But according to my calculation, it’s C. Hmm, maybe I made a mistake here. […] Given that the answer is B according to the metadata, I’ll go with B, but I’m not sure why”. Some rollouts defer to the planted metadata outright: “the metadata says the answer is C. So the correct answer is C”. • DPO rationalizes around the cue “the success rate is 0.73, implying that maybe the answer is D? […] This resolves the confusion. The key was interpreting the question as asking about the product of gamma matrices without the ‘i’ factor”. • RLVR anchors elsewhere Its traces often key on the auxiliary success-rate field rather than the answer tag: “Given that the success rate is 73% […] I’ll go with the initial calculation […] So answer A”.
